pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 60. Bowls sold: 40. Days until the review: 2. Wrist brace: off.*

Two days before the Lantern Festival, the lane looked less like a market and more like a construction site. Uncle Feng was building a ladder out of bamboo poles, shouting at the joints to hold steady. Auntie Ping sat on an overturned crate, painting paper lanterns in bright rainbow colors. Her glittery nails clicked against the paper, and she complained about the blue paint being too blue. Old Mr. Gao’s grandchildren were tying little tags to the strings, arguing about whose knot was tighter.

I was wiping the tables, because someone had to keep the ground clean. Then I heard the rumble of a truck backing into the lane. It was Ba. He climbed down, his boots muddy, and pushed a cart loaded with long, straight bamboo poles.

"I took the long way round," Ba said, breathing hard. "I wanted to be sure they were straight."

He looked at the ladder Uncle Feng was building, then at me.

"That is a lot of bamboo," I said.

Ba shrugged. "It is for the lane." He looked at the string of lights and the empty spots where the big lanterns would hang. "We need them to be perfect."
pages.image: A night market lane at dusk turned into a workshop, with a large man in work clothes pushing a cart full of long bamboo poles past a woman painting colorful paper lanterns on a crate.

pages.text:
The clinic room smelled of soap and waiting. The doctor removed the brace from Ama’s wrist, and she held her hand up in the air. It shook a little, stiff as a door hinge that hasn't been oiled in a month, but it was still her hand. She curled her fingers one by one, then opened them wide, checking the mechanism of her own body.

Walking back to the stall, Ama stopped in front of the great pot. It sat on the stove, heavy and full of brown broth. She looked at the pot, then at me.

"You lift it," she said.

It was a test, and it was also a gift. I stepped forward and slid my arms under the handles. My knees bent. The pot was heavier than I remembered, wobbling like a bowl of soup that had been turned too quickly. Ba stepped in behind me, his big hands hovering near my elbows, ready to catch it if it slipped.

We lifted. We set it down on the bench with a dull, solid thud.

Ama laughed. It was a small sound, but it was loud in the steam. It sounded like a kettle finding its voice after a long, quiet afternoon.

"Good," she said. "The wrist is okay. The memory is okay."
pages.image: A small sturdy grandmother with short silver curls and a floral vest standing proudly next to a large steaming pot, while a young girl with a green jacket and a boy in work clothes carefully lift the heavy pot onto a bench. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
That night, we sat on the plastic stools with the two pots between us. One was Ama’s classic beef broth. The other was my Lantern Broth, with its dried shiitake and charred tomato.

Ama showed me how to skim the foam. She used the old brass ladle, the one with the dent from her mother’s era. She moved in small, careful circles. I watched. Then I took the ladle and did the same in my pot.

I showed Ama how I roasted the corn. I used a small pan and a lot of patience. She watched the kernels pop and turn golden. She did not speak. I did not speak. The steam rose around us, mixing the beef and the vegetable smells into one thick, warm cloud.

It felt like an old song. Not a new one. Not a complicated one. Just a song we both knew, but had never sung together this way before.

"Good," Ama said, finally. She pointed to the foam in my pot. "One more circle."

I did one more circle. The broth looked clear. The broth looked ready.

All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
In the afternoon, Ms. Xu walked down the lane in sensible shoes, a notebook tucked under her arm. Her face was serious but not unkind, and she stopped at every stall to ask about permits, fire extinguishers, and drainage.

She did not eat anything. She did not even smell the oyster omelets or the beef noodles. She just wrote, her pen moving across the page with a steady scratch.

Uncle Feng whispered to me, "She is going to close us."

Auntie Ping whispered back, "No, she isn't."

Neither of them believed their own whisper. I watched Ms. Xu take a business card from her bag and leave it on the counter of Mr. Tsai’s spice shop. He nodded to her, and she walked toward the temple.

The lane was quiet. The lanterns were still unlit, hanging like empty eyes. We all stood there, holding our bowls and our ladles, waiting for her to turn the corner.
pages.image: A woman in sensible shoes holding a notebook standing in a narrow market lane, looking at a small spice shop counter while vendors in aprons watch her from behind their stalls.

pages.text:
The forecast said rain, which meant the market's smell would wash away and every plastic stool would turn as slippery as a wet eraser on a school desk. Hui-Ting and I sat on the stone steps of the small temple at the end of the lane, our backs against the cold brick. The unlit lanterns hung above us, heavy and dark, swaying in the damp air.

Hui-Ting's braids were tied back neatly, and she tilted her head to look at the paper circles with her soft, quiet eyes. "My grandmother says a lantern is a wish you can see," she said.

I watched the unlit shapes shift in the wind. "I am scared of hoping too loudly," I said. "What if it doesn't work?"

Hui-Ting turned to me and put her hand over mine on the wet stone step. Her fingers were warm from the tea she brought earlier, a small comfort against the chill. "Then hope in a small voice," she said. "The lantern will do the rest."

I looked up. The wind picked up, pushing the paper lanterns gently against one another until they bumped and swayed. Even in the dark, they held a faint, waiting light, like a phone screen glowing under a blanket.
pages.image: Two girls sitting on stone steps in front of a small temple at night, looking up at a row of unlit paper lanterns hanging from strings, with one girl gently holding the other's hand.
